title: 2 Chronicles
subtitle: Solomon's Temple, the kings of Judah, and the call to return
lead: 2 Chronicles carries on the story of 1 Chronicles, which was once the same book. It opens with Solomon, who asks God for wisdom, builds the Temple in Jerusalem and dedicates it with a long prayer, and fire comes down from heaven. Then it follows the kings of Judah, one after another, for about four hundred years, until Babylon burns the Temple and takes the people into exile.

Much of the book is copied from 1 and 2 Kings, and its changes show what it cares about. The northern kingdom of Israel drops out of the story except where it touches Judah. Solomon's sins are left out. Good kings like Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah get long chapters of reform and worship, and wicked Manasseh repents. Written for Jews back from exile, the book ends with the Persian king Cyrus telling God's people to go up and build his house again.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): Ezra wrote Chronicles. Most scholars today speak of an unnamed "Chronicler," probably a Levite or Temple writer in Jerusalem, and many think Ezra and Nehemiah come from a different hand.

Written after the return from exile: most scholars say about 400–300 BC; some date it as early as 520 BC or as late as about 250 BC. The story runs from Solomon's accession (about 970 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC), with a closing look at Cyrus's decree (538 BC).
Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah, seen from the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud) after the exile.
Historical narrative, much of it drawn from 1 and 2 Kings, with long prayers and speeches (6; 20:5–12), prophets' sermons (15:1–7; 16:7–9), building accounts, Temple lists and a closing decree.
Late Biblical Hebrew, with spellings and words of the Persian period.

36 chapters, 822 verses. 1 and 2 Chronicles were one book in Hebrew, Divre ha-Yamim, "the events of the days." The Greek calls it Paraleipomena, "things left out." The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) and most printed Hebrew Bibles put it last, so the Hebrew Bible ends with 36:23; the Aleppo and Leningrad codices put it first among the Writings instead.

audience.to: The same first readers as 1 Chronicles, since the two were one book. They were the Jews of the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud) and its rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem, probably about 400–300 BC. They were the heirs of the exiles who came back from Babylon, living under a Persian governor. They had priests and Levites but no king, a modest Temple, and neighbors who also claimed the name Israel.
audience.why: To show that the Temple they worshiped in stood in line with Solomon's, and that the way the kings of Judah rose and fell was a lesson for them. Solomon's prayer (6) and God's answer (7:14) set the rule: when God's people humble themselves, pray, seek him and turn back, he hears and heals. The rest of the book tests that rule on almost every king, and prophets keep explaining it. Knowing the readers changes the reading. The kings' speeches and prayers were spoken to armies, assemblies and Levites. But they are written for a people with no king and no army, whose real defense was worship, the law and seeking the LORD (20:20). Hezekiah's call to the north (30) invites all Israel back to Jerusalem. The exile is told as a Sabbath rest for the land (36:21). The book ends with Cyrus's word, 'let him go up,' a summons the readers had already answered and were still answering.
views: Traditional readers, following the Talmud (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), hold that Ezra wrote Chronicles about 450–400 BC for the community he led. The shared ending and beginning with Ezra (36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–3) fit this view.
The late Persian or early Greek period

Most scholars, such as Japhet, Williamson and Klein, date the book about 400–300 BC. They read it for a settled Temple community in Yehud, taught by Levites and learning from the kings how to seek the LORD.
As in 1 Chronicles, a few scholars place a first edition about 520–515 BC, in Zerubbabel's day (Cross, Freedman). Some date the book as late as about 250 BC, under the Ptolemies.

Some scholars read the pattern of reward and punishment as a rigid theology imposed on history. Others, such as Dillard and Japhet, stress that warnings almost always come first, and read it as a call to repent addressed to the readers.
Hope for David's line, or not

Williamson and others hear a living hope for a son of David. Others think the Chronicler had accepted Persian rule and saw the Temple as the lasting form of David's kingdom; the ending with Cyrus can be read either way.
Older scholars saw an anti-Samaritan book. Most now, following Williamson, see a book that calls northerners back to Jerusalem (11:16; 30:6–9) while rejecting the northern kingdom's worship.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Chronicles is a faithful second history, drawn from Kings and from the other records it names, such as the writings of Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo (9:29), Shemaiah (12:15), Jehu son of Hanani (20:34) and Isaiah (26:22; 32:32). The Talmud names Ezra as its writer (Bava Batra 15a), and the Hebrew Bible places it last.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars date Chronicles to the Persian or early Greek period (about 400–250 BC) and read it as a deliberate rewriting of Kings for the returned community in Judah. It follows only the kings of Judah, rewards and punishes each generation in its own lifetime, and centers on the Temple. Scholars debate how much of its extra material (Manasseh's repentance, Hezekiah's Passover, the building notices) rests on older sources.

lenses.name: Beside Kings
lenses.desc: 2 Chronicles copies, trims and adds to Kings, and the changes are the clearest window into its purpose: the northern kingdom drops out except where it touches Judah, Solomon's sins are left out, Hezekiah and Josiah gain whole chapters of reform, and Manasseh repents (33:12–13). Where the Hebrew of the two books matches, this site uses the same English, so the differences show.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis prize Chronicles for its picture of Temple worship and read its additions as a store of lessons; Manasseh's repentance became the model that no sinner is beyond return (Sanhedrin 101b–103a). The book closes the Hebrew Bible with Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem (36:23).

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Christians read Solomon's Temple and God's promise to David's line as pointing to Christ, the true Temple and the son of David. The Prayer of Manasseh, written to fill in 33:12–13, is in the Orthodox Bible and the Apocrypha, and Jesus' words about Zechariah killed between the altar and the Temple (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51) are often traced to 24:20–22.

authorship: The Talmud says that Ezra wrote "the genealogy of Chronicles up to his own time" (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). Many traditional Jewish and Christian readers have held that Ezra, the priest and scribe who came to Jerusalem about 458 BC (Ezra 7:1–10), compiled both books of Chronicles from Samuel–Kings and from the records of prophets they name, such as Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo (9:29) and Isaiah (26:22; 32:32). The last verses of 2 Chronicles (36:22–23) are repeated at the start of Ezra (Ezra 1:1–3), which fits this view.

Most scholars speak of "the Chronicler," an unnamed writer, probably a Levite connected with the Temple, working in Jerusalem about 400–300 BC. As with 1 Chronicles, the evidence is the late Hebrew, the interest in Levites and singers, and the line of David running past the exile (1 Chronicles 3:19–24). Since Sara Japhet (1968) and H. G. M. Williamson (1977), most think Ezra–Nehemiah comes from a different hand, though the shared ending and beginning show the books were linked early. Others still defend a common author or school. Some scholars think the closing decree of Cyrus (36:22–23) was added from Ezra when the books were arranged.

2 Chronicles names about a dozen sources: "the book of the kings of Judah and Israel" in several forms, and the records of prophets and seers, among them Shemaiah and Iddo (12:15), Jehu son of Hanani (20:34) and Isaiah (32:32). Scholars debate whether these were separate works, sections of Kings, or the Chronicler's way of claiming prophetic authority for his history. Many accept that he had some old material beyond Kings, such as Rehoboam's fortress list (11:6–10) and Hezekiah's tunnel (32:30), while others see most of the additions as his own.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Key terms match the rest of the site: YHWH is "the LORD"; hesed is "loyal love" (1:8; 5:13; 6:42); ma'al is "act unfaithfully" (12:2); nagid is "ruler" (6:5); chozeh is "visionary" (9:29; 12:15); and torah is "law" (6:16; 12:1).

Parallel passages

More than half of 2 Chronicles has a twin in 1 or 2 Kings. Where the Hebrew of Chronicles is the same as its parallel, the Plain uses the site's wording of Kings exactly, so a reader comparing the two sees only the real differences. Where the Hebrew differs, the English differs too, and a note or variant says whether the difference is Chronicles' own change, a different text of Kings, or a copying slip. Solomon's closing lines in 6:41–42 adapt Psalm 132:8–10 and are translated from Chronicles' own Hebrew.

The text

The Hebrew of Chronicles is generally well preserved, but its numbers and some rare words suffered in copying, and its Masoretic notes correct the written text in places (9:29; 11:18). The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex except where a variant explains otherwise, as at 1:13, 6:42 and 10:14. The Greek translation, Paraleipomena, is a separate translation from the Greek of Kings and is often a good witness to an older Hebrew text; where it is cited, the variant says whether its reading was checked directly in Rahlfs' edition or taken from the commentaries.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book has two parts. Chapters 1–9 tell Solomon's reign almost entirely as the building and dedication of the Temple, with his wisdom and wealth as the frame. Chapters 10–36 follow the kings of Judah from the split of the kingdom to the fall of Jerusalem, one reign at a time. The northern kingdom appears only where it touches Judah. Four reigns receive the most space: Jehoshaphat (17–20), Hezekiah (29–32) and Josiah (34–35), each a reformer, and Manasseh, whose repentance is told only here (33). The book ends with the exile as the land's Sabbath rest and with Cyrus's call to rebuild the house of God (36:20–23).

A small group of words carries the book's message. Kings who seek the LORD (darash) prosper; those who act unfaithfully (ma'al) fall. When trouble comes, the way back is to humble oneself, pray and turn. God states the pattern to Solomon (7:14), and the rest of the book tests it on almost every king, beginning with Rehoboam (12:1–12). Scholars call this the Chronicler's doctrine of immediate retribution, because results come within the same lifetime, often explained by a prophet. Some read it as a rigid theology imposed on history. Others stress that it is a call to repent, since nearly every judgment is preceded by a warning and can be turned back.

Traditional readers hold that Chronicles adds true information from the sources it names, and that its differences from Kings are inspired explanations or come from other records. They point to details confirmed outside the Bible, such as Shishak's campaign (12:2–9) and Hezekiah's tunnel (32:30). Critical scholars since de Wette and Wellhausen have often treated the additions as the Chronicler's own theology in story form: Manasseh's repentance, Uzziah's skin disease as punishment, huge armies and sudden victories. Many today take a middle view: the Chronicler had some old sources beyond Kings, such as lists of fortresses and building works, but shaped his whole history to teach his own generation.

Chronicles' silences are as telling as its additions. It does not tell of Solomon's struggle for the throne, his many foreign wives (only Pharaoh's daughter appears, at 8:11) or his idols (1 Kings 1–2; 1 Kings 11). Nor does it tell the northern kingdom's history or, apart from a letter of Elijah (21:12–15), the stories of Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 12–2 Kings 17). Readers explain this in several ways. Many scholars see an ideal David-and-Solomon age, kept clean as a model for the Temple. Traditional readers note that Chronicles assumes its readers know Kings (see 10:15, which presupposes 1 Kings 11:29–39), and that a writer may choose what serves his purpose. Others point out that the book is not simply flattering: it adds sins to the records of Asa, Joash, Amaziah and Uzziah, and it judges Rehoboam plainly (12:14).

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read 2 Chronicles
sections.b:
The Talmud places Chronicles last (Bavli Bava Batra 14b), and so do most printed Hebrew Bibles, so the Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's call to the exiles to go up to Jerusalem. The Aleppo and Leningrad codices, the manuscripts this translation follows, put Chronicles first among the Writings instead. Jewish tradition draws on Solomon's prayer for its practice of praying toward Jerusalem (Berakhot 30a), and on Manasseh's repentance as proof that no one is beyond return (Sanhedrin 101b–103a).

The Greek Bible places the book after Kings under the title Paraleipomena, "things left out," and Christian readers long treated it as a supplement. Christians read the promise to David's house (6:16; 7:18) as fulfilled in Christ, the true son of David, and the Temple filled with glory as a figure of Christ and his people. Jesus' words about "the blood of Zechariah" (Luke 11:51) are often traced to 24:20–22. The Prayer of Manasseh, written to fill in 33:12–13, is in the Orthodox Bible and the Apocrypha. Christians also quote 7:14 widely in calls to national prayer.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the Temple as the book's main character
spec.body: My own reading: in 2 Chronicles the Temple, more than any king, is the main character. The book opens with it planned and built (2–4), filled with glory (5–7) and set in order (8). Every later reign is measured by what the king does to it: Asa and Jehoshaphat honor it, Joash repairs it, Ahaz shuts its doors, Hezekiah cleanses and reopens it, Manasseh fills it with idols, Josiah restores its worship, and Nebuchadnezzar burns it (36:19). The last word of the book is the command to build it again (36:23). Read this way, the kings come and go around a single house, and the story's hope rests on the house being rebuilt. Much of this overlaps published work. Many commentators note the frame from Solomon's decision to build (2:1) to Cyrus's command to rebuild (36:23), and Japhet (The Ideology of the Book of Chronicles), Dillard and Selman (in their introductions) show that each king is measured by his care for the Temple and its worship. What I add is the framing: the house itself as the book's main character, with a story of its own from founding to burning to the call to rebuild.

prompts:
A great stone courtyard before a tall cedar-and-stone temple with two bronze pillars at its porch. On a huge bronze altar, piled sacrifices burst into flames as a column of fire pours down from a darkening sky. Priests in white linen stagger back from the temple door, which is hidden in bright cloud. Across the pavement a vast crowd kneels with faces to the ground. A king in a plain robe kneels on a low square bronze platform in the middle of the court, his palms raised. Levite singers at one side hold lyres and cymbals.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.
The queen of Sheba arrives in Jerusalem (9:1–4)

A long caravan of camels winds up toward a walled hilltop city, loaded with bundles of spices, chests and jars. At its head a dark-skinned queen in layered robes and a tall headdress rides beneath a fringed canopy, attendants with fans beside her. At the city gate a young king waits with courtiers and guards holding gold-covered shields. Behind the walls, the roof of a great temple and a long cedar hall rise above the houses.

reading: Sara Japhet, I and II Chronicles (Old Testament Library, 1993)
A major critical commentary, careful on the Chronicler's sources, his changes to Kings and his ideas.
H. G. M. Williamson, 1 and 2 Chronicles (New Century Bible, 1982)
A compact, balanced commentary, strong on the book's purpose and its relation to Kings.
A detailed critical commentary, especially good on the Hebrew text, the Greek and the parallels.
Raymond B. Dillard, 2 Chronicles (Word Biblical Commentary, 1987)
An evangelical commentary that takes the Chronicler's theology of reward and repentance seriously and fairly.
Martin J. Selman, 2 Chronicles (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries, 1994)
A short evangelical commentary that reads Chronicles as an interpretation of the earlier history.
John C. Endres, William R. Millar and John Barclay Burns, eds., Chronicles and Its Synoptic Parallels (1998)
Chronicles printed side by side with Kings and the other parallels in English.
